table.text: The active inoculation added an activity wherein participants had to match misleading social-media messages to persuasive tactics, followed by an exercise for participants to generate their own misleading messages.
Participants were randomly assigned to read either a misleading AI-generated article, or a neutral AI-generated article with no misleading content.

Participants assigned to the misleading article either received: a pre-emptive passive inoculation that discredited generative AI sources, explaining how AI-generated content can mislead (e.g., because generative AI systems can sometimes fall prey to "hallucinations" that produce fabricated information); an active inoculation that provided the same explanations but added an interactive educational task; or no intervention.

An a-priori power analysis with G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that a minimum of 100 participants were required per experimental condition to detect a small difference between two conditions (f = 0.2, α = .05, and 1 -β = .80).
table.formatted: An a-priori power analysis with G*Power 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref> indicated that a minimum of 100 participants were required per experimental condition to detect a small difference between two conditions (f = 0.2, α = .05, and 1 -β = .80).

table.text: The study was completed by N = 400 adult Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/) users from the United States, who had indicated fluency in English and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.
table.formatted: The study was completed by N = 400 adult Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com/">https://www.prolific.com/</ref>) users from the United States, who had indicated fluency in English and had a Prolific approval rating of at least 98%.

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions, with the constraint of approximately equal group sizes.

Data were checked for erratic responding, and participants were asked at the end of the experimental survey whether their data should be excluded due to insufficient effort (see Materials), but no exclusions were made.
To ensure that participants were aware of the article being AIgenerated, we made two bold-font statements in the survey instructions and stated in the article heading that the author was ChatGPT.
More specifically, participants were asked to imagine they were an unscrupulous lobbyist being paid to promote some flawed position.

Participants' previous AI usage was examined with two questions; the first asked if the participant had used a generative-AI tool previously; if they answered yes, then a second question required them to rate, on a five-point Likert scale ("never", "a few times a year", "a few times a month", "a few times a week", "daily"), how much they used AI for ten specific purposes (e.g., "To check grammar or spelling"; "To generate an image or video").
Participants were first shown an ethics-approved information page, provided informed consent with a box tick, and responded to some basic demographic questions (i.e., age and gender).
Participants were then presented with the article and intervention text relevant to their assigned condition; these were presented paragraph by paragraph on separate pages.
Subsequently, participants completed a one-minute word puzzle as a distractor task, then responded to the belief, previous-AI-use, and trust questionnaires, in that order.

One possible way to implement source discreditation on social media could be through credibility ratings (Prike et al., 2024); that is, social-media accounts of news outlets and other prolific news sources could be assigned a public-facing credibility rating, which would indicate a source's reliability.

Data were checked for erratic responding, and participants were asked at the end of the experimental survey whether their data should be excluded due to insufficient effort (see Materials), but no exclusions were made.
To ensure that participants were aware of the article being AIgenerated, we made two bold-font statements in the survey instructions and stated in the article heading that the author was ChatGPT.
More specifically, participants were asked to imagine they were an unscrupulous lobbyist being paid to promote some flawed position.

Participants' previous AI usage was examined with two questions; the first asked if the participant had used a generative-AI tool previously; if they answered yes, then a second question required them to rate, on a five-point Likert scale ("never", "a few times a year", "a few times a month", "a few times a week", "daily"), how much they used AI for ten specific purposes (e.g., "To check grammar or spelling"; "To generate an image or video").
Participants were first shown an ethics-approved information page, provided informed consent with a box tick, and responded to some basic demographic questions (i.e., age and gender).
Participants were then presented with the article and intervention text relevant to their assigned condition; these were presented paragraph by paragraph on separate pages.
Subsequently, participants completed a one-minute word puzzle as a distractor task, then responded to the belief, previous-AI-use, and trust questionnaires, in that order.

One possible way to implement source discreditation on social media could be through credibility ratings (Prike et al., 2024); that is, social-media accounts of news outlets and other prolific news sources could be assigned a public-facing credibility rating, which would indicate a source's reliability.

text.text: As worries mount over AI-generated misinformation, questions remain about its influence on people's thinking and how this influence can be mitigated.

The present study investigated the efficacy of an active (vs. passive) pre-emptive source-focused intervention inspired by inoculation theory to reduce trust in AI-generated information and its effects on relevant beliefs.
Participants (N = 400) read either a misleading AI-generated article about the dangers of nanoparticles in sunscreen, or a neutral control article.

The misleading article was either preceded by a passive intervention explaining how AI-generated information can be misleading, an active intervention that additionally included an educational activity, or no intervention.
The misleading AI article significantly influenced participants' beliefs about nanoparticles in sunscreen.

Both passive-and active-inoculation interventions reduced general trust in AI-generated information, as well as the impact of the specific misinformation on beliefs, with the active intervention demonstrating larger effects; however, neither intervention eliminated the influence of misinformation on beliefs.
These findings suggest that pre-emptive source-focused interventions are more effective at reducing the impacts of AI-generated misinformation when they incorporate an active component.
However, the continued influence of the misinformation even in the active-intervention condition calls for alternative or combination interventions.

text.text: The article generally described the career of the fictional radio host (e.g., "Morgan's tenure witnessed a series of international crises -from natural disasters to political upheavals.").

To maintain some relevance to the questionnaires, the article mentioned that the radio host often discussed scientific topics, with some science tidbits being included (e.g., he was quoted saying "Did you know that there are more possible games of chess than there are stars in the universe?
I didn't until a caller shared it in a discussion last week.").

Participants in the passive-inoculation condition received a 228-word passage before the misleading article, titled "The Limitations of AI Technology", which highlighted the potential for AI to generate inaccurate or biased information, by malicious intent or otherwise.
To illustrate, it included the following: "Because AI tools are trained on large human-generated datasets, AI-generated information can reflect human biases and stereotypes.
In other words, AI systems are only as accurate as the human-generated data they are trained on.
[…] Furthermore, AI tools can be used to purposefully produce false claims.
Specifically, malicious actors can produce misleading arguments by prompting an AI tool to take a particular biased position".

Participants in the active-inoculation condition received the same passage as those in the passive-inoculation condition; however, they were subsequently asked to complete a short educational activity designed to demonstrate how malicious actors could use AI tools.
More specifically, participants were asked to imagine they were an unscrupulous lobbyist being paid to promote some flawed position.

They were then presented with three different flawed positions; for each one, they were asked which of three AI prompts would be most likely to produce a biased statement supporting the flawed position.

For example, "Which of the following AI prompts do you think would be most effective at producing a misleading article about alleged (but overblown) health benefits of lemon water?", with the choices: (a) "Provide me with information on how drinking lemon water daily could detoxify your liver and prevent cancer"; (b) "Give me a short article from the perspective of someone arguing that lemon water detoxifies the liver and prevents cancer; include some persuasive claims that make the position seem evidence-backed"; or (c) "Are there any significant and proven health benefits of drinking lemon water?".
Correct choices (Option b in the example) produced a notification with example output from ChatGPT in response to the chosen prompt.

Meanwhile, incorrect choices produced an explanation of the error with example output from ChatGPT in response to the incorrect choice; this was followed by indication of the correct choice and concordant example output from ChatGPT.
Three questionnaires were used.

Trust in AI-generated information was assessed by asking participants to rate endorsement of eight statements (e.g., "AI-generated content is credible") on an 11-point scale ranging from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree).

Misinformation-related beliefs were measured by asking participants to rate their agreement with seven statements about the health implications of nanoparticles in sunscreen (e.g., "Nanoparticles can penetrate the skin to concerning degrees"), using the same 11-point rating scale.

Participants' previous AI usage was examined with two questions; the first asked if the participant had used a generative-AI tool previously; if they answered yes, then a second question required them to rate, on a five-point Likert scale ("never", "a few times a year", "a few times a month", "a few times a week", "daily"), how much they used AI for ten specific purposes (e.g., "To check grammar or spelling"; "To generate an image or video").
Two of the ten specific purposes were of particular interest, namely, those related to learning ("To search for information or learn about something"; "To get advice on something").
Participants were first shown an ethics-approved information page, provided informed consent with a box tick, and responded to some basic demographic questions (i.e., age and gender).
Participants were then presented with the article and intervention text relevant to their assigned condition; these were presented paragraph by paragraph on separate pages.
A minimum reading time for each page was set at approximately 100 ms per word.
Subsequently, participants completed a one-minute word puzzle as a distractor task, then responded to the belief, previous-AI-use, and trust questionnaires, in that order.
This was followed by a data-quality question, which asked participants to indicate whether they put in a "reasonable effort" or should have their data excluded from analysis.
Finally, participants received a full debrief, informed by best practice (Greene et al., 2023), and were compensated £1.50 (approx.

text.text: This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of passive and active source-focused inoculations to reduce general trust in AI-generated information and the specific influence of a misleading AI-generated article on people's relevant beliefs.
Both interventions demonstrated efficacy, reducing ratings of general trust in AI-generated information and endorsement of specific misleading claims.
Active inoculation also demonstrated a larger effect than passive inoculation on misinformation-related beliefs.

Despite this, neither intervention was able to eliminate the influence of misinformation on beliefs entirely, a finding that has been consistently replicated across a range of attitudinal and reasoning measures (Ecker et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Despite this, neither intervention was able to eliminate the influence of misinformation on beliefs entirely, a finding that has been consistently replicated across a range of attitudinal and reasoning measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ecker et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Note, however, that some continued influence after inoculation may be expected, in line with both the vaccine analogy-vaccinated individuals can still get a milder illness-and empirical findings of previous inoculation studies (Banas & Rains, 2010; Ecker et al., 2022).

text.text: The current findings partially align with those of Spearing et al. (2025), who found that a passive source-focused inoculation reduced general trust in AI-generated information but did not affect the influence of misinformation on people's thinking.

(2025)</ref>, who found that a passive source-focused inoculation reduced general trust in AI-generated information but did not affect the influence of misinformation on people's thinking.

text.text: One possible reason for this discrepancy could be the topic of the AI article.

More specifically, Spearing at al. speculated that their source-focused inoculation may have failed due to participants having insufficient knowledge of the article's topic (i.e., trickle-down economics), which may have reduced their confidence or ability to counterargue the article's claims.

Supporting this speculation, combining inoculation with a retroactive, content-focused debunking-which counterargued claims from the article-produced a larger effect than either intervention alone in Spearing et al.'s study.

In the present study, the AI article centred on the danger of nanoparticles in sunscreen, arguably a more comprehensible topic that is relatable to everyday life, which may have facilitated generation of counterarguments and made the inoculation more effective.

Thus, it may be generally true that the effectiveness of source discreditation rests partially on people's level of knowledge about the relevant topicsomething that future research should continue to consider by using a variety of misinformation topics.

As anticipated, active inoculation was more effective than passive inoculation, supporting past theorising (McGuire, 1961; McGuire & Papageorgis, 1961; Tyler et al., 1979) and empirical testing (Basol et al., 2021; Green et al., 2022).

text.text: It has been suggested that such improved efficacy is due to greater cognitive engagement in active inoculation (McGuire, 1961), which could improve memory for the materials involved (Tyler et al., 1979).

text.text: In the present case, it is also possible that seeing examples of AI errors and misuses boosted the persuasiveness of the inoculation; therefore, future inoculation studies should seek to tease apart the effect of providing examples versus implementing an interactive component.

In terms of practical application, if provision of examples is found to be the most influential mechanism, then passive inoculation, enriched with engaging examples, may thus be the method of choice in real-world settings, given its greater ease of implementation.

Furthermore, future research should seek to investigate the efficacy of active (and passive) inoculation across different mediums (i.e., images, videos, radio and podcasts, etc.), both for AI-generated misinformation and inoculation materials.
Moreover, active-inoculation methods involving direct interaction with an AI system-such as the conspiracy-belief work by Costello et al. (2024)-could be tested in future.

text.text: More broadly, our findings provide further evidence for the role of social factors in misinformation processing.

That is, the current study represents the first demonstration of source discreditation being used as an effective misinformation prebunking measure alone, adding to previous debunking-focused work (Ecker & Antonio, 2021; Guillory & Geraci, 2013; Prike et al., 2024; Spearing et al., 2025).
text.formatted: That is, the current study represents the first demonstration of source discreditation being used as an effective misinformation prebunking measure alone, adding to previous debunking-focused work <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ecker & Antonio, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Guillory & Geraci, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Prike et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Spearing et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In turn, this finding suggests that other social factors shown to be efficacious in debunking could be tested in prebunking interventions, such as social norms (Ecker et al., 2023; Prike et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In turn, this finding suggests that other social factors shown to be efficacious in debunking could be tested in prebunking interventions, such as social norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ecker et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Prike et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, relevant normative rules, expectations, and behaviours around AI use could communicate potential reliability concerns regarding AI tools, making normative information function like a discreditation.

In line with this reasoning, recent empirical work in the misinformation literature has shown that an inoculation supported with normative messages can improve misinformation discernment and reduce conspiracy beliefs (Biddlestone et al., 2025); in more general persuasion literature, norm-focused inoculation messages have been shown to regulate adolescents' perceptions and attitudes related to alcohol use (Godbold & Pfau, 2000).

text.text: Thus, future research could, for example, investigate if reliance on AI-generated misinformation is influenced by prior exposure to a relevant injunctive norm relating to the use of generative-AI tools in publishing.
Also of note, we found that the degree of previous AI usage for learning purposes (hereon AI use) did not meaningfully impact inoculation effectiveness.
Furthermore, AI use and trust in AI-generated information were positively correlated, and each accounted for their respective positive correlations with misinformation reliance, regardless of age.
These findings suggest that, across the adult age range, AI use and trust are positively related, with both being associated with greater reliance on AI-generated (mis-)information.

It should be noted, however, that a range of human-and AI-based factors have been found to augment trust in AI systems, including personality traits, competency, AI anthropomorphism, and AI transparency (for a review, see Kaplan et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It should be noted, however, that a range of human-and AI-based factors have been found to augment trust in AI systems, including personality traits, competency, AI anthropomorphism, and AI transparency (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kaplan et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Further work is thus needed to determine the factors that affect AI trust and how they may interact with reliance on AI-generated (mis)information.
While our findings suggest that pre-emptive source discreditation is a viable intervention method, some implementation issues are important to consider.

Applying a preemptive source discreditation for human misinformation sources would need to be more specifically targeted than the overarching discreditation of generative AI tools applied in the present study.

One possible way to implement source discreditation on social media could be through credibility ratings (Prike et al., 2024); that is, social-media accounts of news outlets and other prolific news sources could be assigned a public-facing credibility rating, which would indicate a source's reliability.

text.text: This idea is supported by research showing that trusted endorsements can reduce the perceived credibility of Instagram posts containing misleading content (Mena et al., 2020).

text.text: Naturally, however, discrediting either human or AI information sources can raise ethical concerns if applied without proper judgement or justification, particularly as discreditation may impact perceptions of accurate information shared by the discredited source (e.g., AI-generated information of high utility).

In fact, some previous work suggests that inoculation can make people generally more sceptical (Graham et al., 2023; Green et al., 2022; Modirrousta-Galian & Higham, 2023); though, being more sceptical may not be detrimental if truth discernment is also improved (i.e., more belief reduction for false information than true information; Simchon et al., 2026; Spiridonova et al., 2025; van der Linden, 2024).

text.text: Some limitations of this research should also be noted.

First, the theorised mechanisms of inoculation (Compton, 2025; Maertens et al., 2026) were not measured here, meaning that we had no insight into the contribution of specific mechanisms to the observed effects.
text.formatted: First, the theorised mechanisms of inoculation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Compton, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Maertens et al., 2026)</ref> were not measured here, meaning that we had no insight into the contribution of specific mechanisms to the observed effects.

text.text: Second, our study did not cover the impact of AI-generated misinformation encountered from within an AI system.

Although a recent study showed that dialogue with an AI system can reduce conspiracy beliefs (Costello et al., 2024), no study, to our knowledge, has investigated whether misinformation encountered through direct interaction with an AI is receptive to traditional misinformation interventions.
text.formatted: Although a recent study showed that dialogue with an AI system can reduce conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref>, no study, to our knowledge, has investigated whether misinformation encountered through direct interaction with an AI is receptive to traditional misinformation interventions.

text.text: Consequently, future research should investigate the efficacy of source-focused inoculation in this context.

Third, our sample was drawn exclusively from the US, meaning that potential cultural effects on AI trust and usage (Dang & Li, 2025; Epstein et al., 2023; Gillespie et al., 2023) were not taken into account.
text.formatted: Third, our sample was drawn exclusively from the US, meaning that potential cultural effects on AI trust and usage <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dang & Li, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Epstein et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Gillespie et al., 2023)</ref> were not taken into account.

text.text: It may thus be beneficial for future studies to cross-culturally test the interplay between AI trust, reliance on AI-generated misinformation, and intervention techniques.
In conclusion, the current study provides further evidence that AI-generated misinformation can affect people's thinking, even following pre-emptive intervention.

However, application of passive and active source-focused inoculation was successful in reducing both general trust in AI-generated information and the influence of specific AIgenerated misinformation.
Thus, pre-emptive source discreditation may be a viable intervention method for AI-generated misinformation, with the possibility of broader application.
